# D2. Numerical checks {#num}

Section {{< var p.sec_numerical >}} of the paper computes date-specific Markov policy functions by backward induction
along the demographic transition, and tests every candidate equilibrium at each state; the technical documentation
[@BergGE26doc] gives the algorithms. The first table compares the date-specific solution with a time-invariant policy
function, the approximation of much of the quantitative politico-economic literature, at the same dates. The second
counts, by the solves that wrote them, and the third, for every file of results that records them, the equilibria and
the candidates found at any state, and the states at which no candidate passed the test; appendix
{{< var p.app_T >}} of the paper states these counts for the paper's results. There the solver falls back on a rule of the technical documentation: it ranks the candidate taxes by the
integral of the first order condition, and the designs by the political objective with each design at its own
consistent distribution of savings. The tables record a fallback only in the choice of the design. A single
equilibrium at every state means that the selection rule of section {{< var p.sec_numerical >}} never had to choose.

## The horizon and the terminal condition {#num-horizon}

Appendix {{< var p.app_T >}} of the paper solves the calibrated economies again with the backward induction
started two periods earlier, three periods later and under its steady-state terminal condition, and reports the
outcomes in the calibration year and one period later. The table gives the change against the paper's horizon at
every date to the last dated period. Under log preferences the U.S. outcomes do not depend on the horizon. Elsewhere
a longer horizon or the steady-state terminal condition moves the tax rate by a few hundredths of a percentage
point at most at any date, and the chosen design by less than a thousandth. A horizon two periods shorter moves the
outcomes of the calibration year as little, but those of the last dated periods by more, since its terminal period
is then close. At the paper's horizon every date it reports is within a few hundredths of a percentage point of its
value under the steady-state terminal condition.
